claim: Functional connectivity patterns are shaped largely by the relatively stable underlying skeleton of structural connections.
source: It is thought that functional connectivity patterns are shaped largely by the relatively stable underlying skeleton of structural connections (O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Reilly et al., 2013

claim: Modifications in functional connectivity might be influenced by changes in synaptic efficacy through changes in the quantity of neurotransmitter release, changes in astrocytes or dendritic spine stabilization.
source: However, modifications in functional connectivity might also be influenced by changes in synaptic efficacy, for example through changes in the quantity of neurotransmitter release, changes in astrocytes or dendritic spine stabilization.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanisms

claim: Repetitive paired-pulse TMS with a brief inter-pulse interval (8 ms) evokes synchronous pre- and post-synaptic activity.
source: We demonstrate that paired transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) near ventral premotor cortex (PMv) and primary motor cortex (M1) with a short 8-ms inter-pulse interval evoking synchronous pre- and post-synaptic activity and which strengthens interregional connectivity between the two areas in a pattern consistent with Hebbian plasticity, leads to increased functional connectivity between PMv and M1 as measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
evidence: Based on the experimental design and known properties of paired-pulse TMS

claim: Paired-pulse TMS with 8 ms IPI strengthens interregional connectivity between PMv and M1 in a pattern consistent with Hebbian plasticity.
source: We demonstrate that paired transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) near ventral premotor cortex (PMv) and primary motor cortex (M1) with a short 8-ms inter-pulse interval evoking synchronous pre- and post-synaptic activity and which strengthens interregional connectivity between the two areas in a pattern consistent with Hebbian plasticity, leads to increased functional connectivity between PMv and M1 as measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
evidence: Experimental finding from the study

claim: Paired-pulse TMS with 8 ms IPI leads to increased functional connectivity between PMv and M1 as measured with fMRI.
source: We demonstrate that paired transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) near ventral premotor cortex (PMv) and primary motor cortex (M1) with a short 8-ms inter-pulse interval evoking synchronous pre- and post-synaptic activity and which strengthens interregional connectivity between the two areas in a pattern consistent with Hebbian plasticity, leads to increased functional connectivity between PMv and M1 as measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
evidence: Primary experimental finding from the study

claim: Strengthening connectivity between PMv and M1 has effects on a wider network of areas, such as decreasing coupling in a parallel motor programming stream.
source: Moreover, we show that strengthening connectivity between these nodes has effects on a wider network of areas, such as decreasing coupling in a parallel motor programming stream.
evidence: Experimental finding from the study

claim: Identical TMS pulses at identical frequencies with a 500 ms inter-pulse-interval caused no change in fMRI-measured functional connectivity.
source: A control experiment revealed that identical TMS pulses at identical frequencies caused no change in fMRI-measured functional connectivity when the inter-pulse-interval was too long for Hebbian-like plasticity.
evidence: Control experiment finding

claim: Statistical dependencies between remote cortical regions exist both in the absence of external stimuli or task demands (during the resting state) and during execution of a task.
source: Statistical dependencies between remote cortical regions exist both in the absence of external stimuli or task demands (i.e., during the resting state) and during execution of a task (Hampson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hampson et al., 2002

claim: Functional connectivity has been used to identify pathological changes occurring in neural circuits in conditions such as stroke.
source: In addition to providing insights into the basic anatomical and physiological organization of healthy neural networks (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Smith et al., 2009; O'Reilly et al., 2013), functional connectivity has been used to identify pathological changes occurring in neural circuits in conditions such as stroke (Wang et al., 2010), traumatic brain injury (Bonnelle et al., 2011; Ham and Sharp, 2012), neurodegeneration (Seeley et al., 2009), or psychiatric disorders (Bassett et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2010

claim: Functional connectivity has been used to identify pathological changes occurring in neural circuits in traumatic brain injury.
source: In addition to providing insights into the basic anatomical and physiological organization of healthy neural networks (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Smith et al., 2009; O'Reilly et al., 2013), functional connectivity has been used to identify pathological changes occurring in neural circuits in conditions such as stroke (Wang et al., 2010), traumatic brain injury (Bonnelle et al., 2011; Ham and Sharp, 2012), neurodegeneration (Seeley et al., 2009), or psychiatric disorders (Bassett et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonnelle et al., 2011 and Ham and Sharp, 2012

claim: Functional connectivity has been used to identify pathological changes occurring in neural circuits in neurodegeneration.
source: In addition to providing insights into the basic anatomical and physiological organization of healthy neural networks (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Smith et al., 2009; O'Reilly et al., 2013), functional connectivity has been used to identify pathological changes occurring in neural circuits in conditions such as stroke (Wang et al., 2010), traumatic brain injury (Bonnelle et al., 2011; Ham and Sharp, 2012), neurodegeneration (Seeley et al., 2009), or psychiatric disorders (Bassett et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Seeley et al., 2009

claim: Functional connectivity has been used to identify pathological changes occurring in neural circuits in psychiatric disorders.
source: In addition to providing insights into the basic anatomical and physiological organization of healthy neural networks (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Smith et al., 2009; O'Reilly et al., 2013), functional connectivity has been used to identify pathological changes occurring in neural circuits in conditions such as stroke (Wang et al., 2010), traumatic brain injury (Bonnelle et al., 2011; Ham and Sharp, 2012), neurodegeneration (Seeley et al., 2009), or psychiatric disorders (Bassett et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bassett et al., 2008

claim: Repetitive paired pulses of TMS with a brief inter-pulse interval (8 ms) modulate synaptic efficacy in a specific corticocortical pathway.
source: To this aim, we modulated synaptic efficacy in a specific corticocortical pathway using repetitive paired pulses of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with a brief inter-pulse interval (IPI; 8 ms) that evoked synchronous pre- and post-synaptic activity and monitored whether those changes were reflected in altered functional connectivity (Experiment 1) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Experimental design and methodology

claim: Several TMS protocols have been shown to induce changes in excitability in primary motor cortex (M1) using repetitive stimulation of M1 itself.
source: Several TMS protocols have been shown to induce changes in excitability in primary motor cortex (M1) using repetitive stimulation of M1 itself (Chen et al., 1997) or stimulation of premotor regions projecting to M1 (Munchau et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 1997

claim: TMS protocols have been shown to induce changes in excitability in primary motor cortex (M1) using stimulation of premotor regions projecting to M1.
source: Several TMS protocols have been shown to induce changes in excitability in primary motor cortex (M1) using repetitive stimulation of M1 itself (Chen et al., 1997) or stimulation of premotor regions projecting to M1 (Munchau et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Munchau et al., 2002

claim: Changes in M1 excitability induced by TMS are often thought to reflect frequency-dependent potentiation of synaptic transmission.
source: These changes are often thought to reflect frequency-dependent potentiation of synaptic transmission.
evidence: Interpretation based on established knowledge

claim: Repetitive paired stimulation of an input into M1 (such as the median nerve) and then of M1 itself can change M1 cortico-spinal excitability.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that repetitive paired stimulation of an input into M1—such as the median nerve—and then of M1 itself can change M1 cortico-spinal excitability (Stefan et al., 2000; Wolters et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stefan et al., 2000 and Wolters et al., 2003

claim: Paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocols are based upon Hebbian principles of synaptic plasticity.
source: These paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocols are based upon Hebbian principles of synaptic plasticity and appear to modify connectivity in a controlled manner.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PAS protocols

claim: Paired-pulse TMS over interconnected sites (homotopical M1 sites) demonstrated altered motor cortical excitability.
source: Investigations that applied paired-pulse TMS over interconnected sites—for example, homotopical M1 sites (Rizzo et al., 2009), M1 and the supplementary motor area (SMA) (Arai et al., 2011), and M1 and posterior parietal cortex (Koch et al., 2013)—demonstrated altered motor cortical excitability.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rizzo et al., 2009

claim: Paired-pulse TMS over M1 and the supplementary motor area (SMA) demonstrated altered motor cortical excitability.
source: Investigations that applied paired-pulse TMS over interconnected sites—for example, homotopical M1 sites (Rizzo et al., 2009), M1 and the supplementary motor area (SMA) (Arai et al., 2011), and M1 and posterior parietal cortex (Koch et al., 2013)—demonstrated altered motor cortical excitability.
evidence: Supported by citation to Arai et al., 2011

claim: Paired-pulse TMS over M1 and posterior parietal cortex demonstrated altered motor cortical excitability.
source: Investigations that applied paired-pulse TMS over interconnected sites—for example, homotopical M1 sites (Rizzo et al., 2009), M1 and the supplementary motor area (SMA) (Arai et al., 2011), and M1 and posterior parietal cortex (Koch et al., 2013)—demonstrated altered motor cortical excitability.
evidence: Supported by citation to Koch et al., 2013

claim: The repetitive paired-pulse TMS protocol induces a causal and directional change of influence of PMv over M1.
source: Notably, the current protocol of repetitive paired-pulse TMS has been shown to induce a causal and directional change of influence of the first brain region (ventral premotor cortex: PMv) over the anatomically connected second region (M1) (Buch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buch et al., 2011

claim: Pathway-specific changes occur in animal models of synaptic plasticity.
source: This is important since it is such pathway-specific changes that occur in animal models of synaptic plasticity (Markram et al., 1997; Jackson et al., 2006) and these are argued to underlie the self-organization proposed to occur in mono-synaptically connected networks in response to regularly occurring input (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Markram et al., 1997 and Jackson et al., 2006

claim: Pathway-specific changes underlie the self-organization proposed to occur in mono-synaptically connected networks in response to regularly occurring input.
source: This is important since it is such pathway-specific changes that occur in animal models of synaptic plasticity (Markram et al., 1997; Jackson et al., 2006) and these are argued to underlie the self-organization proposed to occur in mono-synaptically connected networks in response to regularly occurring input (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sussillo and Abbott, 2009

claim: PMv and M1 are part of the dorsolateral circuit of areas composed of the anterior intraparietal (AIP) area, areas PF and PFG in the inferior parietal lobule, and PMv and M1 in the frontal lobes.
source: PMv and M1 are a part of the so-called 'dorsolateral circuit' of areas composed of the anterior intraparietal (AIP) area, areas PF and PFG in the inferior parietal lobule, and PMv and M1 in the frontal lobes.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: During complex motor behaviour such as reaching and grasping, the dorsolateral sensorimotor stream is complemented by a dorsomedial circuit composed of dorsal premotor (PMd), medial intraparietal area (MIP), and posterior superior parietal cortex (pSPL).
source: During complex motor behaviour such as reaching and grasping this dorsolateral sensorimotor stream is complemented by a 'dorsomedial circuit' composed of dorsal premotor (PMd), medial intraparietal area (MIP), and posterior superior parietal cortex (pSPL) (Jeannerod et al., 1995; Wise et al., 1997; Tanne-Gariepy et al., 2002; Galletti et al., 2003; Brochier and Umiltà, 2007; Grafton, 2010; Turella and Lingnau, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The connections between premotor cortex and M1 are glutamatergic, excitatory ones.
source: As is the case for other inter-regional connections, the connections between premotor cortex and M1 are glutamatergic, excitatory ones, but there are synapses on both pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons within M1 (Tokuno and Nambu, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tokuno and Nambu, 2000

claim: There are synapses from premotor cortex on both pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons within M1.
source: As is the case for other inter-regional connections, the connections between premotor cortex and M1 are glutamatergic, excitatory ones, but there are synapses on both pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons within M1 (Tokuno and Nambu, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tokuno and Nambu, 2000

claim: Paired stimulation of PMv and M1 leads to strengthening of the excitatory connections between PMv and M1.
source: This means that although paired stimulation of PMv and M1 leads to strengthening of the excitatory connections between PMv and M1, such strengthening can lead to both enhanced facilitatory and enhanced inhibitory influences of PMv on M1.
evidence: Inference from the experimental design and known anatomy

claim: Strengthening of PMv-M1 connections can lead to both enhanced facilitatory and enhanced inhibitory influences of PMv on M1.
source: This means that although paired stimulation of PMv and M1 leads to strengthening of the excitatory connections between PMv and M1, such strengthening can lead to both enhanced facilitatory and enhanced inhibitory influences of PMv on M1.
evidence: Inference from anatomical knowledge about synaptic targets

claim: Enhanced facilitatory influences of PMv on M1 are more apparent when subjects are subsequently tested while performing a simple reaching and grasping task.
source: Enhanced facilitatory influences are more apparent when subjects are subsequently tested while performing a simple reaching and grasping task, and enhanced inhibitory influences are more apparent when subjects are subsequently tested while at rest (Buch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buch et al., 2011

claim: Enhanced inhibitory influences of PMv on M1 are more apparent when subjects are subsequently tested while at rest.
source: Enhanced facilitatory influences are more apparent when subjects are subsequently tested while performing a simple reaching and grasping task, and enhanced inhibitory influences are more apparent when subjects are subsequently tested while at rest (Buch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buch et al., 2011

claim: The different effects of paired stimulation appear as a function of the subject's behavioural and cognitive state at the time of testing.
source: These different effects appear as a function of the subject's behavioural and cognitive state at the time of testing (Bäumer et al., 2009; Buch et al., 2010), but they have not been shown to depend on the subject's cognitive state at the time of plasticity induction (Buch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bäumer et al., 2009 and Buch et al., 2010

claim: The effects of paired stimulation have not been shown to depend on the subject's cognitive state at the time of plasticity induction.
source: These different effects appear as a function of the subject's behavioural and cognitive state at the time of testing (Bäumer et al., 2009; Buch et al., 2010), but they have not been shown to depend on the subject's cognitive state at the time of plasticity induction (Buch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buch et al., 2011

claim: PMv microwire stimulation in macaques has been shown to exert both facilitatory and inhibitory effects on corticospinal outputs as a function of the animal's state.
source: PMv microwire stimulation in macaques has also been shown to exert both facilitatory and inhibitory effects on corticospinal outputs as a function of the animal's state (Prabhu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prabhu et al., 2009

claim: Classic Hebbian synaptic learning rules such as pathway specificity, spike timing dependency, rapid evolution, persistence for several hours, and reversibility have been demonstrated for the PMv-M1 pathway manipulation.
source: Classic Hebbian synaptic learning rules such as pathway specificity, spike timing dependency, rapid evolution, persistence for several hours, and reversibility have been demonstrated for this directed pathway manipulation.
evidence: Based on previous characterization of the TMS protocol

claim: Lesions and disruption of brain areas can affect distant areas and connections.
source: Recent studies have shown that lesions and disruption of brain areas as well as lesions to connections between brain areas can affect distant areas and connections (O'Shea et al., 2007; Hartwigsen et al., 2012; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Shea et al., 2007, Hartwigsen et al., 2012, and O'Reilly et al., 2013

claim: Activity in contralateral non-dominant PMd is increased after interruption of ipsilateral PMd.
source: For example, in the study by O'Shea et al. (2007), it is suggested that 'activity' in contralateral 'non-dominant' PMd is increased after interruption of ipsilateral PMd.
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Shea et al., 2007

claim: Enhancement of contralateral PMd is accompanied by preserved performance in a stimulus-response matching task.
source: This enhancement of contralateral PMd is accompanied by preserved performance in a stimulus-response matching task.
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Shea et al., 2007 in context

claim: Action reprogramming can be preserved after PMd interference if the supramarginal gyrus is uncompromised.
source: Similarly, Hartwigsen et al. (2012) show that action reprogramming can be preserved after PMd interference if the supramarginal gyrus is uncompromised.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hartwigsen et al., 2012

claim: The interruption of specific pathways has effects far beyond the regions that are directly connected by the pathway.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that the interruption of specific pathways has effects far beyond the regions that are directly connected by the pathway (O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Reilly et al., 2013

claim: 90 paired pulses were applied over ventral frontal cortex near PMv and M1 at 0.1 Hz for 15 min.
source: 90 paired pulses were applied over ventral frontal cortex near PMv and M1 (mean MNI coordinates [−56 19 19] and [−40 −18 59] respectively) at 0.1 Hz for 15 min.
evidence: Experimental protocol described in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The mean MNI coordinates for PMv stimulation were [−56 19 19].
source: 90 paired pulses were applied over ventral frontal cortex near PMv and M1 (mean MNI coordinates [−56 19 19] and [−40 −18 59] respectively) at 0.1 Hz for 15 min.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: The mean MNI coordinates for M1 stimulation were [−40 −18 59].
source: 90 paired pulses were applied over ventral frontal cortex near PMv and M1 (mean MNI coordinates [−56 19 19] and [−40 −18 59] respectively) at 0.1 Hz for 15 min.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Repeated paired TMS led to an increase in PMv-M1 BOLD functional connectivity while participants performed the task.
source: Repeated paired TMS led to an increase in PMv-M1 BOLD functional connectivity while participants performed the task (paired t-test: t(13) = -2.59, p = 0.023; Figure 2C), while PMv-M1 BOLD coupling at rest was not modulated by the intervention (t(14) = -0.07, p = 0.94; Figure 2F).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: PMv-M1 BOLD coupling at rest was not modulated by the intervention.
source: Repeated paired TMS led to an increase in PMv-M1 BOLD functional connectivity while participants performed the task (paired t-test: t(13) = -2.59, p = 0.023; Figure 2C), while PMv-M1 BOLD coupling at rest was not modulated by the intervention (t(14) = -0.07, p = 0.94; Figure 2F).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The responsiveness of M1 to input from PMv increases following paired TMS of the areas.
source: Using a psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analysis (Friston et al., 1997; O'Reilly et al., 2012), we confirmed that the responsiveness of M1 to input from PMv increases following paired TMS of the areas.
evidence: PPI analysis of experimental data

claim: Increases in connectivity between the stimulated areas (psychophysiological interactions) support the notion that PMv has a greater influence on M1 after repeated paired stimulation during performance of the prehension task.
source: Increases in connectivity between the stimulated areas (psychophysiological interactions) support the notion that PMv has a greater influence on M1 after repeated paired stimulation during performance of the prehension task (paired t-test: t(13) = −4.78, p = 0.0004; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of PPI data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The relationship between activity in PMv and M1 did not change in the resting state condition following the plasticity-inducing TMS intervention.
source: PPI analysis of resting state fMRI data confirmed that the relationship between activity in PMv and M1 did not change in that condition following the plasticity-inducing TMS intervention (t(14) = 0.08, p = 0.93; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of PPI data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: PMv-M1 coupling was increased following repeated stimulation of those areas during grasping task performance.
source: Functional coupling measured during grasping task performance confirmed that PMv-M1 coupling was increased following repeated stimulation of those areas (PMv-M1: t(13) = -3.72, p = 0.003).
evidence: Statistical analysis of partial correlation data

claim: At rest, repeated paired TMS led to increased dorsolateral circuit coupling between AIP and PMv.
source: At rest, repeated paired TMS led to increased dorsolateral circuit coupling (AIP-PMv: t(14) = -2.50, p = 0.025; Figure 3), but decreased dorsomedial circuit coupling (PMd-pSPL: t(14) = 2.22, p = 0.04; PMd–M1: t(14) = 2.84, p = 0.013; Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis of partial correlation data shown in Figure 3

claim: At rest, repeated paired TMS led to decreased dorsomedial circuit coupling between PMd and pSPL.
source: At rest, repeated paired TMS led to increased dorsolateral circuit coupling (AIP-PMv: t(14) = -2.50, p = 0.025; Figure 3), but decreased dorsomedial circuit coupling (PMd-pSPL: t(14) = 2.22, p = 0.04; PMd–M1: t(14) = 2.84, p = 0.013; Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis of partial correlation data shown in Figure 3

claim: At rest, repeated paired TMS led to decreased dorsomedial circuit coupling between PMd and M1.
source: At rest, repeated paired TMS led to increased dorsolateral circuit coupling (AIP-PMv: t(14) = -2.50, p = 0.025; Figure 3), but decreased dorsomedial circuit coupling (PMd-pSPL: t(14) = 2.22, p = 0.04; PMd–M1: t(14) = 2.84, p = 0.013; Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis of partial correlation data shown in Figure 3

claim: Functional connectivity involving area V3A did not change following repeated paired TMS applied to the PMv-M1 pathway.
source: Finally, functional connectivity involving area V3A, a relatively early visual area that links to both the dorsomedial and dorsolateral circuits, did not change following repeated paired TMS applied to the PMv-M1 pathway (V3A-AIP: t(14) = 0.51, p = 0.618; V3A-pSPL: t(14) = 1.45, p = 0.170).
evidence: Statistical analysis of partial correlation data

claim: M1 becomes more responsive to inputs from PMv during task performance following repeated stimulation of those areas in Experiment 1.
source: The analysis corroborated the finding that M1 becomes more responsive to inputs from PMv during task performance following repeated stimulation of those areas in Experiment 1 (PMv-M1: t(13) = -2.53, p = 0.0064).
evidence: Statistical analysis of multiple regression data

claim: Within the dorsolateral circuit, PMv became more responsive to inputs from AIP at rest following paired-pulse TMS.
source: Within the dorsolateral circuit, PMv became more responsive to inputs from AIP (AIP-PMv: t(14) = -2.55, p = 0.023; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,D,E); this finding is in line with our results from the partial correlation analysis (Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis of multiple regression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The multiple regression analysis confirmed the decreased interaction of PMd and M1 within the dorsomedial circuit.
source: The multiple regression analysis also confirmed the decreased interaction of PMd and M1 within the dorsomedial circuit (PMd–M1: t(14) = 2.84, p = 0.013; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,D,E); the response of PMd to activity in pSPL showed a tendency to be decreased (PMd-pSPL: t(14) = 1.78, p = 0.097; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D,E).
evidence: Statistical analysis of multiple regression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The response of PMd to activity in pSPL showed a tendency to be decreased following paired-pulse TMS.
source: The multiple regression analysis also confirmed the decreased interaction of PMd and M1 within the dorsomedial circuit (PMd–M1: t(14) = 2.84, p = 0.013; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,D,E); the response of PMd to activity in pSPL showed a tendency to be decreased (PMd-pSPL: t(14) = 1.78, p = 0.097; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D,E).
evidence: Statistical analysis of multiple regression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: During performance of the grasping task, a significant increase in activation of the left intraparietal sulcus area AIP and the adjacent supramarginal gyrus (SMG) was observed following TMS.
source: During performance of the grasping task, a significant increase in activation of the left intraparietal sulcus area AIP [−44 −40 46] and the adjacent supramarginal gyrus (SMG) [−62 −34 34] was observed following TMS (Figure 4A; blue regions, p = 0.012; t-statistic images were subjected to cluster-based thresholding and corrected for multiple comparisons for a one-sided t-test at t > 1.76 with alpha-level p ≤ 0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of dual-regression data shown in Figure 4A

claim: AIP and SMG, after paired TMS and during grasping, showed significantly more co-activation with the sensorimotor network.
source: This means that AIP and SMG, after paired TMS and during grasping, showed significantly more co-activation with what has previously been called the 'sensorimotor network' (Smith et al., 2009; Power et al., 2011) (red-to-yellow region, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which includes much of motor and premotor cortex and interconnected regions of parietal cortex (Tomassini et al., 2007; Mars et al., 2011).
evidence: Interpretation of dual-regression results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, supported by citations

claim: At rest, pathway potentiation evoked coactivation of PMv and a prefrontal region close to the site of stimulation (inferior frontal junction, IFJ).
source: During rest, an analogous exploratory analysis revealed increased activity in IFJ, and adjacent areas 44d and PMv [−56 4 30] (Figure 4B; blue regions, p = 0.007; cluster-based thresholding and multiple comparison-correction for one-sided t-test at t > 1.76 with alpha-level p ≤ 0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of dual-regression data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The IFJ is a key prefrontal transitional region involved in high-level control of the motor system and interacts prominently with PMv, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and visual association areas in the occipitotemporal cortex.
source: The IFJ is a key prefrontal transitional region involved in high-level control of the motor system and interacts prominently with PMv, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and visual association areas in the occipitotemporal cortex (Neubert et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neubert et al., 2014

claim: Regions IFJ, area 44d, and PMv become more coupled with the rest of the left-lateralised frontoparietal network following repeated paired-pulse TMS.
source: Regions IFJ, area 44d, and PMv are part of a left-lateralised 'frontoparietal network' (red-to-yellow region, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and the results mean that they become more coupled with the rest of this network following repeated paired-pulse TMS.
evidence: Interpretation of dual-regression results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: PMv-M1 coupling was not changed during task performance following paired TMS with a 500 ms IPI.
source: A higher-level analysis of functional connectivity between PMv-M1 confirmed that PMv-M1 coupling was not changed during task performance following paired TMS with a 500 ms IPI; this is in contrast to significantly greater connectivity following paired TMS with an 8 ms IPI (mixed-model ANOVA: TIME by PROTOCOL interaction: F(1,26) = 4.64, p = 0.041; Experiment 2 during task: paired t-test: t(13) = 0.94, p = 0.36).
evidence: Statistical comparison between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2

claim: Functional connectivity was not changed in the PMv-M1 connection following either 8 ms or 500 ms IPI protocol at rest.
source: At rest, functional connectivity was not changed in the PMv-M1 connection following either protocol (Experiment 2 at rest: paired t-test: t(14) = 0.07, p = 0.95).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Experiment 2 data

claim: No changes in coupling in the wider dorsolateral and dorsomedial sensorimotor circuits were found after 500 ms IPI TMS at rest.
source: At rest, no changes in coupling in the wider dorsolateral and dorsomedial sensorimotor circuits were found after 500 ms IPI TMS (Experiment 2 at rest: paired t-tests: AIP-PMv: t(14) = 1.08, p = 0.30; pSPL-PMd: t(14) = -1.24, p = 0.24; PMd-M1: t(14) = 0.47, p = 0.65).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Experiment 2 data

claim: The strengthening of functional connectivity in the AIP-PMv pathway was significantly stronger after 8 ms IPI TMS than after 500 ms IPI TMS.
source: Further statistical testing showed that the strengthening of functional connectivity in the AIP-PMv pathway was significantly stronger after 8 ms IPI TMS (Experiment 1) than was after 500 ms IPI TMS (Experiment 2) (mixed-model ANOVA: TIME by PROTOCOL interaction: F(1,28) = 7.15, p = 0.012) as were the decreases in the PMd-pSPL pathway strength (mixed-model ANOVA: TIME by PROTOCOL interaction: F(1,28) = 5.29, p = 0.029).
evidence: Statistical comparison between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2

claim: The decreases in the PMd-pSPL pathway strength were significantly stronger after 8 ms IPI TMS than after 500 ms IPI TMS.
source: Further statistical testing showed that the strengthening of functional connectivity in the AIP-PMv pathway was significantly stronger after 8 ms IPI TMS (Experiment 1) than was after 500 ms IPI TMS (Experiment 2) (mixed-model ANOVA: TIME by PROTOCOL interaction: F(1,28) = 7.15, p = 0.012) as were the decreases in the PMd-pSPL pathway strength (mixed-model ANOVA: TIME by PROTOCOL interaction: F(1,28) = 5.29, p = 0.029).
evidence: Statistical comparison between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2

claim: The PMd-M1 connection showed a similar trend of stronger decrease after 8 ms IPI TMS than after 500 ms IPI TMS.
source: The PMd-M1 connection showed a similar trend (mixed-model ANOVA: TIME by PROTOCOL interaction: F(1,28) = 5.92, p = 0.08).
evidence: Statistical comparison between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2

claim: It was only after 8 ms IPI TMS in Experiment 1 that the left frontoparietal network was found to be more coherently coupled with itself and co-active with PMv in the resting state.
source: Finally, employing a dual-regression analysis, we confirmed that it was only after 8 ms IPI TMS in Experiment 1 that the left frontoparietal network was found to be more coherently coupled with itself and co-active with PMv in the resting state, but not after 500 ms IPI TMS in Experiment 2 (mixed-model ANOVA: TIME by PROTOCOL interaction: p = 0.022).
evidence: Statistical comparison between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 using dual-regression

claim: The fronto-parietal network did not significantly alter its coupling pattern in Experiment 2.
source: The fronto-parietal network did not significantly alter its coupling pattern in Experiment 2 (p = 0.446).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Experiment 2 dual-regression data

claim: During task performance, the two connectivity measures (TMS-based effective connectivity index and fMRI-based functional connectivity measure) for the PMv-M1 pathway were positively correlated across subjects at baseline.
source: During task performance, the two connectivity measures (a TMS-based effective connectivity index and the fMRI-based functional connectivity measure) for the PMv-M1 pathway were positively correlated across subjects at baseline (Pearson's correlation coefficient: R = 0.74, p = 0.01) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation shown in Figure 5A

claim: A positive correlation between TMS-based and fMRI-based connectivity measures indicates that the greater the facilitatory influence of PMv on M1 as measured with TMS, the greater the fMRI-derived functional connectivity.
source: A positive correlation indicates that the greater the facilitatory influence of PMv on M1 as measured with TMS, the greater the fMRI-derived functional connectivity.
evidence: Interpretation of the correlation result

claim: During task performance, paired-pulse TMS-derived effective connectivity was significantly correlated with fMRI-derived connectivity after repeated paired 8 ms IPI TMS.
source: Furthermore, during task performance, paired-pulse TMS-derived effective connectivity was still significantly correlated with fMRI-derived connectivity after repeated paired 8 ms IPI TMS (R = 0.87, p = 0.0008) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation shown in Figure 5B

claim: At rest, the correlation between TMS-based and fMRI-based connectivity measures was not significant at baseline.
source: At rest, the correlation between the two measures was not significant at baseline (R = −0.21, p = 0.57) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation shown in Figure 5C

claim: At rest, a significant negative correlation was observed between the baseline TMS-derived effective connectivity measure and the fMRI-derived functional connectivity measure following repeated paired 8 ms IPI TMS.
source: However, a significant correlation was observed between the baseline TMS-derived effective connectivity measure and the fMRI-derived functional connectivity measure following repeated paired 8 ms IPI TMS (R = −0.68, p = 0.03) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation shown in Figure 5D

claim: When PMv had a stronger net inhibitory influence on M1 (as indexed by neurophysiological measurements), fMRI indicated stronger net positive functional connectivity between the two areas across participants.
source: Intriguingly, the correlation was negative which implies that when PMv had a stronger net inhibitory influence on M1 (as indexed by neurophysiological measurements), fMRI indicated stronger net positive functional connectivity between the two areas across participants.
evidence: Interpretation of the negative correlation result

claim: Baseline effective connectivity strength at rest (inhibitory) and during grasping (excitatory) were negatively correlated across individuals.
source: Finally, we note that baseline effective connectivity strength at rest (i.e., inhibitory) and during grasping (i.e., excitatory) were also negatively correlated across individuals (R = −0.63, p = 0.049).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation between conditions

claim: Functional connectivity is not only shaped by structural connections but also by short-term plastic changes in synaptic efficacy.
source: From our experiments, we infer that functional connectivity is not only shaped by structural connections but also by short-term plastic changes in synaptic efficacy.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results

claim: Paired stimulation of two brain regions led to increased functional connectivity between the two regions.
source: Paired stimulation of two brain regions led to increased functional connectivity between the two regions but also to a limited set of other functional connectivity changes, both positive and negative, in other parts of the cortical sensorimotor circuits.

claim: Paired stimulation of two brain regions led to a limited set of other functional connectivity changes, both positive and negative, in other parts of the cortical sensorimotor circuits.

claim: Positive functional connectivity between two areas may reflect either facilitatory or inhibitory effective connectivity.

claim: Different patterns of premotor–M1 interaction are seen in patients who do and who do not recover motor skills after stroke.
source: Such changes in functional connectivity are not only interesting in their own right but also because different patterns of premotor–M1 interaction are seen in patients who do and who do not recover motor skills after stroke (Gerloff et al., 2006; Lotze et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gerloff et al., 2006 and Lotze et al., 2006

claim: PMv provides one of the principal inputs into M1 in monkeys.
source: We chose to examine this pathway because it is better understood than many and can be investigated in a number of ways even in humans; in monkeys PMv provides one of the principal inputs into M1, and it exerts a powerful influence over M1 output (Shimazu et al., 2004; Dum and Strick, 2005), and in humans it has been established that paired-pulse TMS of PMv-M1 at an 8 ms IPI, or at similar IPIs, modulates the behavioural and electromyographic (EMG) consequences that are normally observed when M1 is stimulated alone (Davare et al., 2008, 2009; Buch et al., 2010; Neubert et al., 2010; Buch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shimazu et al., 2004 and Dum and Strick, 2005

claim: PMv exerts a powerful influence over M1 output in monkeys.
source: We chose to examine this pathway because it is better understood than many and can be investigated in a number of ways even in humans; in monkeys PMv provides one of the principal inputs into M1, and it exerts a powerful influence over M1 output (Shimazu et al., 2004; Dum and Strick, 2005), and in humans it has been established that paired-pulse TMS of PMv-M1 at an 8 ms IPI, or at similar IPIs, modulates the behavioural and electromyographic (EMG) consequences that are normally observed when M1 is stimulated alone (Davare et al., 2008, 2009; Buch et al., 2010; Neubert et al., 2010; Buch et al., 2011).

source: We chose to examine this pathway because it is better understood than many and can be investigated in a number of ways even in humans; in monkeys PMv provides one of the principal inputs into M1, and it exerts a powerful influence over M1 output (Shimazu et al., 2004; Dum and Strick, 2005), and in humans it has been established that paired-pulse TMS of PMv-M1 at an 8 ms IPI, or at similar IPIs, modulates the behavioural and electromyographic (EMG) consequences that are normally observed when M1 is stimulated alone (Davare et al., 2008, 2009; Buch et al., 2010; Neubert et al., 2010; Buch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

source: This reaching-and-grasping task is known to produce activity in a network of motor and motor association areas including M1 and PMv and also in AIP (Grol et al., 2007).

claim: AIP-PMv-M1 constitute a dorsolateral sensorimotor circuit.
source: Together these areas, AIP-PMv-M1, constitute a dorsolateral sensorimotor circuit.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: The dorsomedial sensorimotor circuit consists of PMd and parietal area pSPL.
source: Another parallel parieto-frontal circuit—the dorsomedial sensorimotor circuit—has also been linked to the control of reaching and grasping and consists of more dorsal areas, including PMd and parietal area pSPL.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: Visual input into the two parallel visuomotor circuits during the task is provided via area V3A.
source: Visual input into the two parallel visuomotor circuits during the task is provided via area V3A.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: Grol et al. (2007) validated a parietal-to-premotor feed-forward network node model in the context of the grasping task using dynamic causal modelling (DCM).
source: Grol et al. (2007) assessed connectivity between these same parietal and premotor areas during performance of the same task, with the same apparatus, as used here. Using dynamic causal modelling (DCM), they validated a parietal-to-premotor feed-forward network node model in the context of the same experimental task that we employ here.
evidence: Supported by citation to Grol et al., 2007

claim: The parietal-to-premotor feed-forward network node model is supported by anatomical evidence of direct projections between AIP-PMv-M1 nodes in the dorsolateral circuit and pSPL-PMd-M1 nodes in the dorsomedial circuit.
source: The model is furthermore supported by other anatomical evidence of direct projections between AIP-PMv-M1 nodes in the dorsolateral circuit and pSPL-PMd-M1 nodes in the dorsomedial circuit (Matelli et al., 1986; Johnson et al., 1997; Wise et al., 1997; Matelli et al., 1998; Luppino et al., 1999; Geyer et al., 2000; Tanne-Gariepy et al., 2002; Dum and Strick, 2005; Rushworth et al., 2006; Grol et al., 2007; Tomassini et al., 2007; Mars et al., 2011; Sallet et al., 2013; Neubert et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple anatomical citations

claim: Resting state and grasping task fMRI data sets were analysed in an identical way but were never compared directly due to categorical differences in movement artefacts.
source: Importantly, resting state and grasping task fMRI data sets were analysed in an identical way but were never compared directly due to categorical differences in movement artefacts which are difficult to disentangle from differences in functional interactions in the cognitive states.
evidence: Methodological decision explained

claim: PMv exerts an inhibitory physiological influence over M1 at rest.
source: It is known that PMv exerts an inhibitory physiological influence over M1 at rest but this turns into a facilitatory influence during grasping (Davare et al., 2008; Buch et al., 2010, 2011).

claim: PMv's inhibitory influence over M1 turns into a facilitatory influence during grasping.

evidence: Supported by citations to Davare et al., 2008 and Buch et al., 2010, 2011

claim: Changes in the interactions between the stimulated areas themselves (PMv and M1) were most apparent when subjects were actively engaged in motor activity.
source: Broadly speaking, changes in the interactions between the stimulated areas themselves, PMv and M1, areas known to be intimately involved in the making of grasping movements, were most apparent when subjects were actively engaged in just such motor activity (Figure 2C, Figure 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Summary of findings across multiple figures

claim: Changes in interactions between PMv and adjacent ventral frontal areas such as IFJ with other prefrontal and parietal areas concerned with high-level cognitive control and attention were more apparent when subjects were at rest.
source: By contrast, changes in interactions between PMv and adjacent ventral frontal areas such as IFJ with other prefrontal and parietal areas concerned with high-level cognitive control and attention were more apparent when subjects were at rest (Figure 4B).
evidence: Summary of findings shown in Figure 4B

source: Changes in interactions between PMv and the parietal areas surrounding AIP were apparent both when subjects were engaged in grasping and when they were at rest (Figure 4A,B).

claim: Similar patterns of fMRI-measured functional connectivity are associated with either net facilitatory or net inhibitory influences being exerted by PMv over M1 when subjects are engaged in a grasping task or at rest.

claim: Subjects with stronger functional connectivity between PMv and M1 also showed higher degrees of TMS-measured effective connectivity between the two areas.

evidence: Summary of correlation findings from Experiment 3

claim: The paired pulse TMS approach provides a particularly direct and simple assay of the effective connectivity that exists between two brain areas.
source: The paired pulse TMS approach provides a particularly direct and simple assay of the effective connectivity that exists between two brain areas but it complements other techniques, such as DCM, that attempt to recover effective connectivity estimates from fMRI data in particular behavioural contexts (Friston, 1994; Friston et al., 2003).
evidence: Methodological statement supported by citations
